lede: Some crystals carry water inside them. This lesson shows how to count it: from a formula, from the masses before and after heating, and on to the empirical formula of any compound from its masses.
can: Define water of crystallisation, hydrated and anhydrous, and work out the Mr of a hydrate.
Heat a hydrated salt to constant mass and use the masses to find x.
Work out empirical and molecular formulae from masses or percentages.

md: Blue copper(II) sulfate crystals turn to a white powder when heated: water locked inside the crystal is driven off. Weighing before and after tells you how much water each unit held.

md: Some salts crystallise with water **chemically bonded into the crystal structure**: **water of crystallisation**. A salt holding it is **hydrated**; with it removed, the salt is **anhydrous**. The dot in a formula counts it.

**See it on washing soda**, $\ce{Na2CO3.10H2O}$:
**1.** The part after the dot gives 10 waters per $\ce{Na2CO3}$.
**2.** Heating to constant mass leaves $\ce{Na2CO3}$, the anhydrous salt.

prompt: What is meant by the term hydrated?
explain: A hydrated salt still holds the water bonded into its crystal, as washing soda holds its 10 waters. Dissolved describes a solution, and a salt with its water removed is anhydrous. Hydrated means it contains water of crystallisation.

prompt: How many water molecules are bonded into the crystal for each MgSO₄ unit in MgSO₄·7H₂O?
explain: Read the number after the dot, as step 1 did for washing soda: 7H₂O means 7 water molecules of crystallisation for every MgSO₄.

alt: A bar for the relative formula mass of CuSO4.5H2O, 250, split into CuSO4, 160, and five waters of 18, 90.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 150" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="hybar"><title id="hybar">A bar for the relative formula mass of CuSO4 with 5 waters, 250, split into the anhydrous salt, 160, and 5 waters of 18 each, 90</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"><rect x="20" y="56" width="360" height="34" rx="3"/><path d="M250.4 56 L250.4 90"/><path d="M20 104 V112 H250.4 V104"/><path d="M250.4 104 V112 H380 V104"/></g><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor"><text x="20" y="30" font-size="14" text-anchor="start" font-weight="600">CuSO₄·5H₂O: Mr 250</text><text x="135.2" y="79" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">CuSO₄</text><text x="315.2" y="79" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">5H₂O</text><text x="135.2" y="132" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">160</text><text x="315.2" y="132" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">5 × 18 = 90</text></g></svg>
caption: The hydrate's Mr is the salt's Mr plus the water's.

md: Add the salt's Mr to the water's. Each $\ce{H2O}$ is $2 \times 1 + 16 = 18$, so n waters add $n \times 18$. Count every atom of the salt first: an oxygen left out cost many candidates the mark in 2025.

title: Why the water counts in the Mr
md: The water is part of the solid: every unit of the crystal carries its waters with it, so a mole of the hydrate weighs the salt plus all of them.

prompt: Using Mg = 24, S = 32, O = 16 and H = 1, work out the Mr of MgSO₄·7H₂O.
explain: Do what the steps did: the salt first, MgSO₄ = 24 + 32 + 4 × 16 = 120; then the water, 7 × 18 = 126; then add them: 246.

text: 3. See it done: x from the Mr

md:
**The question** (2023 shape): hydrated copper(II) sulfate, $\ce{CuSO4.xH2O}$, has Mr 250. Find x. **[3]**
**Step 1.** $\ce{CuSO4}$: $64 + 32 + 4 \times 16 = 160$.
**Step 2.** The water: $250 - 160 = 90$.
**Step 3.** $x = 90 \div 18 = 5$.

prompt: Hydrated cobalt(II) chloride, CoCl₂·xH₂O, has Mr 238. Using Co = 59 and Cl = 35.5, find x.
explain: Follow the three steps: CoCl₂ = 59 + 2 × 35.5 = 130; the water is 238 − 130 = 108; and 108 ÷ 18 = 6. Stopping at 108 gives the water's mass, not x.

md: Heat the hydrated salt in a crucible or an evaporating basin, let it cool, and weigh it. Then **heat, cool and weigh again**, repeating until **two weighings agree**: that is **constant mass**, and it shows all the water of crystallisation has gone. Driving water off by heating is a **thermal decomposition**.

**See the readings**, blue $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$ in a crucible:
**1.** Weigh the empty crucible, then add the salt: 18.42 g, then 20.92 g.
**2.** Heating, cooling and weighing 4 times gives 20.21, 20.05, 20.02, 20.02 g.
**3.** The last 2 readings agree, which makes 20.02 g the constant mass.

prompt: Why is the crucible heated, cooled and weighed again and again until two masses are the same?
options: to make sure all the water of crystallisation has been removed
to let the crucible cool down
to check that the balance is working
answer: to make sure all the water of crystallisation has been removed
explain: While water is still leaving, each heating lowers the mass, as the readings fell from 20.21 g. Once two readings agree, nothing more can be driven off, so all the water of crystallisation has been removed.

md:
**The three masses** a results table asks for:
**Hydrated salt:** 20.92 − 18.42 = 2.50 g.
**Anhydrous salt:** 20.02 − 18.42 = 1.60 g, from the constant mass.
**Water lost:** 2.50 − 1.60 = 0.90 g.
The blue crystals are now a white powder.

prompt: A crucible weighs 21.30 g, with hydrated sodium carbonate 24.16 g, and 22.36 g at constant mass. What mass of water was lost, in g?
explain: Take both masses from the crucible, as the three lines did: the hydrated salt is 24.16 − 21.30 = 2.86 g and the anhydrous salt 22.36 − 21.30 = 1.06 g, so the water is 2.86 − 1.06 = 1.80 g.

alt: One MgSO4 unit beside seven water molecules: 0.02 mol of MgSO4 and 0.14 mol of water, a ratio of 1 to 7.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 170" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="hyrat"><title id="hyrat">One salt unit beside 7 water molecules: 0.02 mol of MgSO4 and 0.14 mol of water, a ratio of 1 to 7</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"><rect x="30" y="66" width="30" height="30" rx="3"/><circle cx="130" cy="70" r="11"/><circle cx="170" cy="70" r="11"/><circle cx="210" cy="70" r="11"/><circle cx="250" cy="70" r="11"/><circle cx="290" cy="70" r="11"/><circle cx="130" cy="104" r="11"/><circle cx="170" cy="104" r="11"/></g><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor"><text x="45" y="50" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">MgSO₄</text><text x="210" y="40" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle" font-weight="600">H₂O</text><text x="45" y="124" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">0.02 mol</text><text x="210" y="138" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">0.14 mol</text><text x="200" y="162" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">0.14 ÷ 0.02 = 7, so 1 : 7</text></g></svg>
caption: x is a ratio of particles, so it comes from moles.

md: The formula counts particles, so x is a **mole** ratio: the moles of water lost divided by the moles of anhydrous salt. Find each with moles = mass ÷ Mr; water's Mr is 18.

title: Divide the moles
md: Summer 2023's C2 Higher report: most found both numbers of moles, but very few went on to divide them to reach x.

prompt: 7.15 g of hydrated sodium carbonate, Na₂CO₃·xH₂O, leaves 2.65 g at constant mass. Using Mr(Na₂CO₃) = 106, find x.
explain: The water is 7.15 − 2.65 = 4.50 g, which is 4.50 ÷ 18 = 0.25 mol. The salt is 2.65 ÷ 106 = 0.025 mol. Divide the water's moles by the salt's: 0.25 ÷ 0.025 = 10.

text: 7. Why x uses moles, not masses

md: Equal masses are not equal numbers of particles. A water molecule has a relative mass of 18; a unit of $\ce{MgSO4}$ has 120, over 6 times as much. So nearly equal masses of salt and water hold very different numbers of particles, and only moles count them.

**Compare them:**
**1.** Masses: 2.40 g against 2.52 g, which gives nearly 1 : 1.
**2.** Moles: $0.02$ against $0.14$, which gives 1 : 7.

prompt: A student divides the mass of water lost by the mass of anhydrous salt to find x. Why does this not work?
options: x is a ratio of particles, and equal masses are not equal numbers of particles
the two masses should be added, not divided
the mass of water should be divided by 16 first
answer: x is a ratio of particles, and equal masses are not equal numbers of particles
explain: Look at the comparison: masses of 2.40 g and 2.52 g are nearly 1 : 1, but the particles are 1 : 7, because each salt unit is much heavier than a water molecule. x counts particles, so it needs moles.

alt: Two iron atoms beside three oxygen atoms in one dashed box, worked from 0.1 mol of iron and 0.15 mol of oxygen: the simplest whole-number ratio, 2 to 3.
svg: <svg viewBox="0 0 400 170" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg" role="img" aria-labelledby="hyemp"><title id="hyemp">2 Fe atoms beside 3 O atoms inside one dashed box: the simplest whole-number ratio, 2 to 3, worked from 0.1 mol and 0.15 mol</title><g fill="none" stroke="currentColor" stroke-width="1.4" stroke-linecap="round"><circle cx="60" cy="80" r="20"/><circle cx="110" cy="80" r="20"/><circle cx="200" cy="80" r="14"/><circle cx="244" cy="80" r="14"/><circle cx="288" cy="80" r="14"/><rect x="24" y="44" width="298" height="72" rx="8" stroke-dasharray="5 4"/></g><g font-family="inherit" fill="currentColor"><text x="60" y="85" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">Fe</text><text x="110" y="85" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">Fe</text><text x="200" y="85" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text x="244" y="85" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text x="288" y="85" font-size="14" text-anchor="middle">O</text><text x="24" y="30" font-size="14" text-anchor="start">Fe: 5.60 ÷ 56 = 0.1 mol</text><text x="24" y="140" font-size="14" text-anchor="start">O: 2.40 ÷ 16 = 0.15 mol</text><text x="24" y="162" font-size="14" text-anchor="start">0.1 : 0.15 = 2 : 3, so Fe₂O₃</text></g></svg>

md: An **empirical formula** is the simplest whole-number ratio of the atoms of each element in a compound; a **molecular formula** gives the actual number of each atom in a molecule. From masses: divide each by its Ar, then by the smallest.

**See it done**: 5.60 g of iron joined with 2.40 g of oxygen.
**1.** Fe: $5.60 \div 56 = 0.1$; O: $2.40 \div 16 = 0.15$.
**2.** Divide by the smaller: $0.15 \div 0.1 = 1.5$, so 1 : 1.5.
**3.** Double to whole numbers: 2 : 3, so $\ce{Fe2O3}$.

md: Percentages work the same way: in 100 g, each percentage is a mass in grams. The molecular formula is a whole number of empirical units, so divide the molecule's Mr by the empirical formula's Mr.

**See it done**: a hydrocarbon of 85.7% carbon and 14.3% hydrogen, Mr 56.
**1.** C: $85.7 \div 12 = 7.14$; H: $14.3 \div 1 = 14.3$.
**2.** $14.3 \div 7.14 = 2$, so $\ce{CH2}$, with Mr 14.
**3.** $56 \div 14 = 4$ units: $\ce{C4H8}$.

prompt: A compound has the empirical formula CH₂ and a relative formula mass of 42. Give its molecular formula.
explain: CH₂ has Mr 14, and 42 ÷ 14 = 3, so the molecule is 3 CH₂ units: C₃H₆.

md: **Define it exactly** (2023, 2024, 2025). Water of crystallisation is water **chemically bonded into the crystal structure**; each half is a mark. Hydrated means it contains water of crystallisation.

**Draw the apparatus** (2022, 2025). A flat, assembled section, as above:
**1.** Basin on gauze on tripod: 3 pieces stacked, which makes the drawing assembled.
**2.** Label every part, Bunsen burner included, which gives 4 labels.

prompt: A question asks you to draw and label the apparatus, set up, for heating a hydrated salt. Which drawing earns the marks?
options: a flat section, assembled, with each piece labelled
the pieces drawn apart, with arrows between them
answer: a flat section, assembled, with each piece labelled
explain: The marks go to recognisable pieces, put together so the apparatus would work, and labelled, as in the basin drawing. The 2025 report found 3-D drawings, four-legged tripods and missing labels losing marks.

md:
**Colours, both ways** (2022 to 2025):
**1.** Heat blue $\ce{CuSO4.5H2O}$: 5 waters leave, which leaves a white powder.
**2.** Add water to white $\ce{CuSO4}$: it turns blue, which gives the test for water.
**The dehydration equation** (2024). Heating $\ce{BaCl2.2H2O}$ gives $\ce{BaCl2 + 2H2O}$: keep the 2.

prompt: A few drops of water fall on anhydrous copper(II) sulfate. What colour change do you see?
explain: Anhydrous copper(II) sulfate is a white powder, and taking water back makes it blue again: white to blue. Heating runs it the other way, and colourless is not the powder's colour.

md: The hardest shape gives only the percentage of the mass left after heating. That percentage is the anhydrous salt's share of the hydrate's Mr, so the Mr follows, and then x.

title: Where the specification stops
md: Naming hydrates with prefixes such as pentahydrate is not required by the CCEA Double Award specification.

prompt: Hydrated iron(II) sulfate, FeSO₄·xH₂O, keeps 54.7% of its mass when heated to constant mass. Using Mr(FeSO₄) = 152, find x.
explain: Follow the steps: the Mr is 152 ÷ 0.547 = 278, so the water is 278 − 152 = 126, and 126 ÷ 18 = 7.

md:
Define water of crystallisation, hydrated and anhydrous; a hydrate's Mr is the salt's + n × 18.
Heat to constant mass and find the masses of salt and water.
Find x: moles of water ÷ moles of anhydrous salt.
Find an empirical formula from masses or percentages, and a molecular formula from the Mr.
Give the colour change both ways, and draw the apparatus flat and labelled.

This is Question 5 of recent C2 papers on both tiers, and practical C5 in Unit 7. Foundation asks for the terms, an Mr, the method, the masses and the colours; Higher adds x and empirical formulae, with working shown. Stuck? Write the three masses first: hydrated, anhydrous and water.
